# `systemd_unit`

`systemd_unit` installs one systemd unit file, or one named drop-in of a
unit, on the node, after systemd's own check (`systemd-analyze verify`)
accepts the new file. It installs units of the kinds `.service`, `.timer`,
`.path`, `.socket`, `.mount`, `.target`, `.swap`, `.slice`, and
`.automount`, templates such as `app@.service` included. A drop-in changes
part of an existing unit, such as a vendor's.

`systemd_unit` only writes the file. [`systemd_service`](systemd_service.md)
starts, stops, enables, and masks the unit, and restarts or reloads it after
a change. For a command on a schedule,
[`systemd_scheduled_job`](systemd_scheduled_job.md) writes a service and its
timer from one node task, and [`cron_job`](cron_job.md) manages a cron entry;
write the units by hand with `systemd_unit` when the service needs settings
those modules do not offer. For a mount kept in `/etc/fstab`, use
[`fstab_mount`](fstab_mount.md), and for a swap file,
[`swap_file`](swap_file.md), which does all the steps.

Keep secret values in a separate private file that the unit references, not
in the unit file.

## Inputs

- `name` (string; required): a unit filename, such as app.service, app@.service, or backup.timer; a .mount is named for its escaped mount point (systemd-escape --path --suffix=mount)
- `drop_in` (string; optional): a single .conf filename; manages `/etc/systemd/system/<name>.d/<drop_in>`
- `in_systemd_of_user_account` (string; optional): an account other than root: the unit belongs to that account's own systemd, its file goes to `<home>/.config/systemd/user/` owned by the account, and MMX turns on lingering for the account so that its units start at boot and keep running after logout
- `content` (string; optional): inline text; exactly one of content or template
- `template` (string; optional): local Go template, relative to the project root, or to the role's directory inside a role; exactly one of content or template
- `state` (`present` or `absent`; default `present`): absent removes only the selected unit file or drop-in and accepts only name, drop_in, in_systemd_of_user_account, and state

## Outputs

The node task's result holds these fields. A later node task reads them as `.node_tasks.<id>.<field>`, where `<id>` is the node task's `id`.

- `status`
- `change`

## What a dryrun reports

Supported; previews contents; validation of a changed unit is not checked.

## Retries and time limits

Bounded automatic retries by default; retry: false turns them off.

The node task takes the time limits `time_limit` and `time_limit_per_try`; without them, the project's `node_task_defaults` apply. `mmx describe-module task` describes the settings every node task accepts.

## Examples

### Change part of a unit with a drop-in

```yaml
- systemd_unit:
    name: app.service
    drop_in: 20-limits.conf     # a drop-in filename you choose
    content: |
      [Service]
      MemoryMax=512M
```

This example manages only
`/etc/systemd/system/app.service.d/20-limits.conf` on the node. Other
drop-ins stay intact. Before replacement, systemd checks the base unit, the
installed drop-ins, and the proposed file together. When systemd rejects the
new file, the existing `20-limits.conf` stays, and the task fails.

### A timer that runs a service

A timer runs a service, usually a oneshot without an `[Install]` section:

```yaml
- task_block:
    id: backup                 # a node task block ID you choose
    changes:
      - systemd_unit:
          name: backup.service
          content: |
            [Service]
            Type=oneshot
            User=backup
            ExecStart=/usr/local/bin/backup
      - systemd_unit:
          name: backup.timer
          content: |
            [Timer]
            OnCalendar=*-*-* 03:00:00
            RandomizedDelaySec=15m
            Persistent=true
            [Install]
            WantedBy=timers.target
    activate:
      - systemd_service:
          name: backup.timer
          start_at_boot: true
          state: running
```

Name the timer, path, or socket in `activate`, rather than the service the
timer, path, or socket starts. Changing a timer, path, or socket definition
makes the `systemd_service` task restart the timer, path, or socket once.

The triggered service needs no node task. Reloading the node's systemd
manager makes the service's next activation use the new service definition.
For `.path` and `.socket` units, also activate the triggering unit and let
the triggered service use the new definition on the next activation.

### A target that restarts a group of services

A target can group services so the services restart together.
In the following example, `PartOf=report-workers.target` makes the two
worker services restart when someone restarts `report-workers.target`.
When the target's definition changes, MMX restarts `report-workers.target`,
which restarts the workers through `PartOf=`.
When `report-worker@.service` changes, MMX restarts the workers through the
two worker `systemd_service` tasks in `activate`:

```yaml
- task_block:
    id: report_workers          # a node task block ID you choose
    changes:
      - systemd_unit:
          name: report-worker@.service
          content: |
            [Unit]
            PartOf=report-workers.target
            [Service]
            ExecStart=/usr/local/bin/report-worker --queue %i
            [Install]
            WantedBy=report-workers.target
      - systemd_unit:
          name: report-workers.target
          content: |
            [Unit]
            Description=Report workers
            [Install]
            WantedBy=multi-user.target
    activate:
      - systemd_service:
          name: report-worker@invoices
          start_at_boot: true
          state: running
      - systemd_service:
          name: report-worker@exports
          start_at_boot: true
          state: running
      - systemd_service:
          name: report-workers.target
          start_at_boot: true
          state: running
```

### A unit in an account's own systemd

Every Linux account can have its own systemd, which runs that account's units
without root. Containers that run without root use the account's systemd.
`in_systemd_of_user_account` on `systemd_unit` and `systemd_service` (and on
[`podman_quadlet`](podman_quadlet.md)) names the account whose systemd owns
the unit, instead of the system's systemd.

Install `/home/reports/bin/report-worker` before the following node task
block:

```yaml
# roles/report_worker/main.yml
node_tasks:
  - user:
      create_home_directory: true
      name: reports
      home: /home/reports
      shell: /bin/sh
  - directory:
      path: /home/reports
      owner: reports
      group: reports
      permissions_mode: "0750"
  - task_block:
      id: report_worker
      changes:
        - systemd_unit:
            name: report-worker.service
            in_systemd_of_user_account: reports
            content: |
              [Service]
              ExecStart=/home/reports/bin/report-worker
              [Install]
              WantedBy=default.target
      activate:
        - systemd_service:
            name: report-worker.service
            in_systemd_of_user_account: reports
            start_at_boot: true
            state: running
```

The unit file goes to `/home/reports/.config/systemd/user/`, owned by
`reports`, and the service runs as `reports`. Everything else works as for a
system unit: drop-ins, the check before installation, the restart after a
changed unit, and `state: absent`.

To look at such a unit by hand, become the account with its runtime
directory set:

```bash
sudo runuser -u reports -- env XDG_RUNTIME_DIR=/run/user/$(id -u reports) \
  systemctl --user status report-worker.service
```

## How it works

### Installation and the check before it

`systemd_unit` takes exactly one of `content` or `template`. It installs a
root-owned `0644` file under `/etc/systemd/system` on the node, through the
`file` module's atomic replacement, after `systemd-analyze verify` accepts
the temporary new file.

That check refuses a unit whose program does not exist yet, with a message
such as `Command /usr/local/bin/myapp is not executable: No such file or
directory`. Put the `systemd_unit` task after the node task that installs
the program, such as a `file`, `unpack_archive`, or package task.

With `drop_in` (a single `.conf` filename), it manages only
`/etc/systemd/system/<name>.d/<drop_in>`, creating that directory when
needed. The new drop-in is checked together with the base unit and the other
installed drop-ins.

### The manager reload and the restart

After a changed unit, MMX runs `systemctl daemon-reload` on the node. An
unchanged unit that is not a template, and each
[`systemd_service`](systemd_service.md) task, also check systemd's
`NeedDaemonReload`. So an interrupted manager reload is recovered through
systemd's own pending-reload state, without a separate MMX record: the next
run reloads systemd for the unchanged file and reports changed, and a dryrun
before it reports `would_change`.

systemd cannot inspect a template as a unit. A template's instances have
their pending manager reload completed by their `systemd_service` node tasks.

Put a unit in the same node task block's `changes` as its service's
configuration
([execution design](../../changing-mmx/design/execution.md#packages-service-definitions-and-checked-out-code)).
Unit and drop-in changes, including removal, are tracked in the service's
definition hash. Within a node task block, they require a restart of the unit
that a `systemd_service` task in `activate` names, even when its configured
refresh is `reload`. Ordinary configuration changes use the service's
selected refresh action instead. The page
[Service recovery](../shared-module-behavior.md#service-recovery) describes the record
of what each service loaded.

### Removal

`state: absent` removes the named complete unit file or drop-in. It accepts
only `name`, `drop_in`, `in_systemd_of_user_account`, and `state`, and removes
only that regular file. It leaves vendor definitions, other drop-ins, and
directories intact.

It does not stop or disable the unit. A decommissioning playbook declares
those service actions first, with a `systemd_service` task, before removing
unit files and accounts. Running it again succeeds when the service is
already stopped and its unit is gone, and also when the account of a unit in
an account's own systemd is gone: such a removal, and such a stop or disable
by `systemd_service`, then reports unchanged.

### Unit kinds and their names

- A `.mount` unit must be named for its escaped mount point:
  `srv-data.mount` for `/srv/data`, and `srv-my\x2ddata.mount` for
  `/srv/my-data`, as `systemd-escape --path --suffix=mount /srv/my-data`
  prints it. systemd's check rejects a mismatched name before installation.
  Starting the mount unit mounts the filesystem at the mount point.
  Enabling the mount unit with an `[Install]` section mounts the filesystem
  at boot.
- A `.swap` and an `.automount` unit are named for their escaped path, like a
  `.mount` unit: `systemd-escape --path --suffix=swap /var/swapfile` prints
  `var-swapfile.swap`.
- An automount needs the `.mount` unit of the same path, and that mount must
  not be mounted when the automount starts.
- `.service`, `.timer`, `.path`, `.socket`, `.target`, and `.slice` units
  need no additional `systemd_unit` YAML fields for the unit kind. What
  [`systemd_service`](systemd_service.md#unit-kinds) does with each kind is on
  its page.

### Units in an account's own systemd

- The unit file goes to `<home>/.config/systemd/user/` of the account, owned
  by the account; a drop-in goes to the matching `.d` directory there.
- The account and its home directory must exist when a task installs a unit
  file. Create them with `user` and `directory` tasks before the node task
  block, as in the example. A removal of a unit file of an account that does
  not exist reports unchanged.
- MMX writes the file as root into the account's home and never follows a
  link there that leads out of the home.
- The account runs systemd's check of its new unit file
  (`systemd-analyze verify --user`), as its own systemd reads its units. MMX
  gives the check a copy of the new file in the
  [node task's private directory](../secrets.md#a-node-tasks-private-directory),
  which is the account's for the check. MMX ends a check that does not end
  within one minute. `podman_quadlet` checks an account's Quadlet file in the
  same way.
- **Lingering.** An account's systemd normally stops when the account's last
  login session ends, and does not start at boot. A task with
  `in_systemd_of_user_account` that installs, starts, or enables a unit turns
  on what systemd calls lingering for the account: its units start at boot
  and keep running after logout. A task that only stops, disables, or removes
  leaves lingering as it is. The task reports it the first time: "Enabled
  lingering for account reports, so its services start at boot and keep
  running after logout". There is no setting for it.
- **While the account's systemd is not running.** With lingering off and
  nobody logged in, the account's systemd does not run, so none of its units
  runs either. A `systemd_service` task that only stops, disables, masks, or
  unmasks then reads and changes whether the unit is enabled or masked in
  the account's unit files themselves (`systemctl --user` with
  `SYSTEMD_OFFLINE=1`). It starts nothing, also in a dryrun, which reports
  what a run would change.
- A unit in an account's systemd is enabled for `default.target`, not
  `multi-user.target`, which belongs to the system.
- Root's units are system units. Validation rejects
  `in_systemd_of_user_account: root`.
- The service record of such a unit is kept for the account and the unit
  together, so `report-worker.service` of two accounts are two services.

### Examples that combine the unit modules

The [application-service example](../../../examples/service-app/README.md) and
the [account-and-unit example](../../../examples/account-and-unit/README.md)
exercise `systemd_unit` together with the account and service modules. The
[limited application controls](../shared-module-behavior.md#limited-application-controls)
use a `.path` unit that `systemd_unit` installs.

## Errors and what they mean

- **`systemd_unit: systemd's check of the new unit file failed: ...`**
  systemd rejected the new file, together with the base unit and the
  installed drop-ins. The installed file stays. Read systemd's words after
  the colon and correct the unit.
- **A drop-in whose base unit is missing.** The run fails as a missing
  prerequisite, and the node task is not tried again. Install the base
  unit, or the package that brings it, in an earlier node task. A dryrun
  reports the check of a changed unit as not checked, because its
  prerequisites may not exist yet. A dryrun previews the contents and writes
  no temporary new unit file.
- **A `.mount`, `.swap`, or `.automount` unit with the wrong name.** systemd's
  check rejects it before installation. Name it as `systemd-escape` prints.
- **`in_systemd_of_user_account: root`.** Validation rejects it. Write the
  unit without the field; it is a system unit.
- **The account's check does not end within one minute.** MMX ends it and
  the task fails. Look for a file in the account's unit directory that is not
  a regular file, such as a named pipe.

## Tested on

**Distributions:** Debian 12 and 13, Ubuntu 24.04 and 26.04, Arch Linux, openSUSE Leap 16.1, Rocky Linux 9, AlmaLinux 10, Fedora 45.

The base suite covers this module (`account_units.py`, `file_resources.py`, `external_modules.py`) and runs on every tested distribution.

The suite `account_units.py` covers every unit kind that `systemd_unit`
installs: a service with a drop-in, a timer, a socket, a mount, a target with
a member service in a slice, an automount, and a swap file. It also covers a
unit in an account's own systemd, whose new file the account itself checks,
with a link in its unit directory to a file that only root can read. The
suite runs in a virtual machine on Debian 12 and 13 and Ubuntu 24.04 and 26.04, because its automount
unit needs autofs, which a container cannot use. `server_resources.py`
covers new unit files and template and alias drop-ins.

The whole catalog runs both suites on Debian 12 and 13 and Ubuntu 24.04 and 26.04
([validation record](../../changing-mmx/validation.md)).

## Why it works this way

- **systemd checks the new file before it replaces the installed one.** A
  unit that systemd rejects never reaches the node's running configuration.
- **An interrupted manager reload needs no MMX record.** systemd's own
  `NeedDaemonReload` says that a reload is still owed.
- **The triggering unit is named in `activate`, not the service it starts.**
  After a changed definition, the manager reload means the service's next
  activation uses the new one.
- **The account itself checks its new unit file, on a copy.** The account
  fills its unit directory, so a check that root ran there would read
  whatever a link in it points to, such as a file that only root may read.
  Root does nothing there by a path either.
- **The account's check ends after one minute at the latest.** A file in the
  unit directory that is not a regular file, such as a named pipe, can make
  systemd wait without end.
- **Lingering is turned on without a setting.** A unit that MMX manages must
  not stop because somebody logged out; the opposite is never what such a
  task means.
